# Only the Hills Will Know

At one o'clock in the afternoon on September 1, 1914, a keeper making his rounds at the Cincinnati Zoological Garden found one of his birds on the floor of her aviary, beneath her perch, and she did not get up. She was very old — around twenty-nine, though no record of her hatching survived — a grey-blue dove with a long, pointed tail, named Martha, after the first First Lady. There was nothing dramatic in the moment. No convulsion, no gathering crowd, no omen in the weather. Just an elderly bird, alone in a cage, stopping.

What makes that moment worth pausing over is arithmetic. With Martha's last breath, the most abundant bird in North America — quite possibly the most abundant bird the Earth has ever known — ceased to exist. Not diminished. Not endangered. Ceased.

It is difficult, now, to hold the numbers in the mind. When Europeans arrived, the passenger pigeon numbered somewhere between three and five billion. By some estimates, that meant one out of every four birds on the continent was a passenger pigeon. In 1871, a single nesting in Wisconsin covered roughly 850 square miles and held an estimated 136 million birds. Flocks passed overhead not for minutes but for days. Hunters spoke of shooting into the mass until their arms tired and the flock above seemed no thinner than when they started. The sun dimmed. Chickens went to roost at noon, believing night had come.

The eyewitness accounts strain toward apocalypse because ordinary vocabulary failed. Alexander Wilson, watching a single flock pass overhead in the first decade of the nineteenth century, timed it hour after hour and finally gave up counting individuals and counted instead the area of sky occupied and the rate of passage. His arithmetic came to something north of two billion birds in one column. In 1813, near Louisville, John James Audubon watched a procession take three full days to pass. "The air was literally filled with pigeons," he wrote; "the light of noon-day was obscured as by an eclipse." The droppings fell like melting snow. The sound of the wings, continuous and enormous, lulled him almost to sleep.

Behind the spectacle was a strange biology. The passenger pigeon was a slender, long-tailed cousin of the mourning dove, built for speed — sixty miles an hour in level flight — and for wandering. It was a nomad of the mast forests, tracking the boom of beechnuts, acorns, and chestnuts across the landscape in vast, unpredictable circuits. Its survival strategy was not hiding or fighting but saturation: appear in such numbers that no predator, no matter how ravenous, could make a dent. Each pair laid a single egg a year, a reproductive rate that looks absurd until you multiply it by billions. Roosting colonies grew so dense that branches snapped under the weight and whole trees came down. Parents fed their chicks crop milk, a secretion rich enough to fatten the young squabs into delicacies that gourmets paid handsomely for. Everything about the species was designed around the assumption that there would always be more.

Recent genomic work adds a twist worth sitting with. A 2017 analysis of passenger pigeon DNA suggested that the species had swung through extreme boom-and-bust cycles for millennia, its numbers surging and collapsing in response to the masting rhythms of the forests themselves. Abundance, in other words, was real — but it was also restless, never guaranteed, a condition the birds maintained rather than possessed. They lived permanently on the high wire. For untold centuries, they stayed on it anyway.

What knocked them off was a machine, assembled with perfect innocence. Two technologies matured together in the middle of the nineteenth century: the telegraph, which could announce a newly discovered nesting ground to the entire eastern seaboard within hours, and the railroad, which could carry the kill to city markets before it spoiled. Before, pigeons had been food for the people who happened to live near them. Suddenly they became a mobile resource, harvested industrially. In 1878, at a giant nesting near Petoskey, Michigan, professional hunters shipped out, by contemporary tallies, something like fifty thousand birds a day, week after week, for the better part of a summer. Birds traveled east packed in barrels of salt or chilled in ice; squabs fetched premium prices; gluts drove the price down to pennies a dozen, and when even the cities couldn't absorb the surplus, pigeons were fed to hogs.

Here is the trap, and it deserves a slow look, because we are still inside versions of it. When a resource appears infinite, its price falls toward zero. And when the price is effectively zero, restraint becomes economically irrational — conservation is charity, and charity doesn't feed a family. Waste cost nothing, so waste was everywhere. James Fenimore Cooper saw the pattern early: *The Pioneers*, published in 1823, contains a famous scene of festival shooters slaughtering thousands of pigeons in an afternoon and leaving the heaps to rot, to the horror of a character who understands that abundance is not the same as license. Cooper was complaining in advance about a century that hadn't happened yet.

The methods refined themselves. Nets were drawn over baited feeding flocks, capturing hundreds in a single pull. Blinded captives, tethered to little platforms, were used as decoys to lure wild birds within reach — a practice so emblematic that it gave the language the phrase "stool pigeon." Hunters burned sulphur beneath nocturnal roosts to stun the birds into falling. Shooting into roosts at dusk was less hunting than shelling. And through it all ran the same serene confidence: there will always be more.

Not everyone shared the confidence. Simon Pokagon, a Potawatomi chief and writer, published an elegy for the pigeon in 1895 describing the slaughter he had witnessed, and he drew the connection that polite society preferred not to draw: a people who had taken pigeons seasonally, sparingly, leaving the great colonies intact for generations, had watched the market economy strip the continent bare within decades — and he recognized in the bird's fate the shape of his own people's dispossession. Both had been treated as inexhaustible. Neither was.

The collapse, when it came, was vertiginous. Through the 1870s the warnings accumulated; through the 1880s the great nestings failed or were destroyed on arrival; the birds grew scarce precisely where they had been thickest. In 1896, one of the last sizable wild gatherings — roughly a quarter-million birds in Ohio — was discovered by sportsmen, and nearly all of them were shot within days. In March 1900, a boy named Press Clay Southworth shot a passenger pigeon near Sargents, in Pike County, Ohio, the last confirmed wild member of the species. His mother, evidently sensing the bird was worth preserving, had it mounted. Consider the asymmetry: the boy did what boys and men had done a million times before, and it happened to be the last time. Nobody in that field knew the label that history would attach to the act. "Last" is a word applied afterward, by people doing arithmetic that participants couldn't yet do.

And then came the phase that should unsettle us most: the refusal to believe. For years afterward, ornithologists chased rumors, offered rewards, investigated reports of flocks "somewhere west." The public preferred explanations of disease, of emigration to South America, of some hidden valley where the storms still gathered. Anything but the truth, which was mundane and unbearable: we killed them, and we cut down the forests that fed them, and there was no secret refuge. Abundance had been read as permanence. The sky had seemed too full to empty.

A few birds survived in captivity, and their story has the sad mechanics of a relay race run in slow motion. A University of Chicago biologist named Charles Otis Whitman kept a small colony through the 1890s, breeding failures stacking on breeding failures, until he resorted to crossing his last passengers with ring-doves — hybrids that inherited neither the wild vigor nor the wild anything of their ancestors. The remnants eventually funneled to the Cincinnati Zoo. By 1909 only a handful remained. In 1910, Martha's last companion died, and for the final four years of the species, she was it. A standing reward of a thousand dollars was offered for a fertile egg — a fortune, then — and it was never claimed. Zookeepers lowered her perch closer to the ground because she no longer flew much. Visitors came to stare. Some were reverent; some, reportedly, threw things.

When she died, the logistics were brisk and oddly dignified. She was packed in a three-hundred-pound block of ice and shipped by express train to Washington, where she was mounted and entered into the Smithsonian's catalogue as specimen 170669. The bird who had been one of billions achieved a different kind of singularity: she outlived her kind by becoming an object.

Thirty-three years later, the Wisconsin Society for Ornithology raised a stone monument to the species at Wyalusing State Park, overlooking the confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers, and asked Aldo Leopold to dedicate it. Leopold, who as a boy had lain awake hoping to hear the thunder of wings that never came, said: "We grieve because no living man will see again the onrushing phalanx of victorious birds, sweeping a path for spring across the March skies... Men still live who, in their youth, remember pigeons. Trees still live who, in their youth, were shaken by a living wind. But a few decades hence only the oldest oaks will remember, and at long last only the hills will know."

He returned to the pigeon in *A Sand County Almanac*, and there he sharpened the point. The specimens in museums, he wrote, are effigies. Book-pigeons cannot dive out of a cloud to startle the deer; they feel no sun, no wind, no weather. "They live forever by not living at all." It is one of the coldest sentences in American nature writing, and it lands cold because it is aimed not at the past but at us — at every species currently sliding from wind into book.

The aftermath rippled outward in ways ecologists are still tracing. The passenger pigeon was a load-bearing element of the eastern forest economy: billions of beaks stripping and redistributing mast, their droppings fertilizing whole regions in pulses. Remove them, and everything downstream shifts. One provocative and still-debated hypothesis even links their disappearance to the modern spread of Lyme disease, reasoning that without pigeons consuming vast acorn crops, white-footed mice — the disease's key reservoir — multiplied unchecked. And there is a bitter coda of timing: in 1904, a decade after the last great flocks vanished, the chestnut blight arrived, and the American chestnut — one of the principal engines of the pigeon's abundance — began its own continental die-off. The birds and their world missed each other going in opposite directions. Any pigeon restored today would find that the forest it was built for no longer exists.

Some people want to try anyway. The nonprofit Revive & Restore, working with geneticist Ben Novak, has pursued a de-extinction project: editing the genome of the band-tailed pigeon, the passenger's closest living relative, stepwise back toward something recognizably passenger-like. Whether it can work is an open technical question. Whether it should is a philosophical one. But notice the deeper problem the project exposes: a species is not only a genome. Migration routes, colony behavior, the knowledge of where the mast runs — these are cultures, transmitted from old birds to young ones. You could hatch a perfect genetic replica and still have produced a creature that is a stranger in its own body, fluent in no tradition, migrating nowhere, because migration was taught, and everyone who could teach it is a hundred years gone.

That may be the passenger pigeon's real bequest: a demonstration that abundance is a story we tell ourselves about the future, not a fact about the present. The same arithmetic that emptied the sky in fifty years is running now against ocean fisheries, against insect biomass, against topsoil. None of it required villains. It required only ordinary decisions — rational at the scale of the individual transaction, catastrophic in aggregate, each one defensible because the supply seemed endless. The pigeoners were not monsters. They were men earning a living, doing math with a denominator set to infinity, and the denominator was wrong.

Today, Martha stands — or hangs, rather — in the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, brought out of the collections regularly, grey-blue and stiff, beside a placard that states the facts plainly, as though plain facts could bear the weight. Schoolchildren press against the glass. Most of them know the story already; it has become one of the parables Americans teach about themselves. And every so often, somewhere in the country, a flock of starlings or blackbirds gathers into a living storm and blacks out a patch of sky, and people stop their cars and stand in parking lots with their mouths slightly open, feeling something older than curiosity move in them — the recognition of what a full sky means, and the faint anxiety of what its emptiness would mean.

Leopold said the hills would be the last to know. Perhaps. But we are not hills. We can still hear the wind come up in the leaves and mistake it, for one glad half-second, for wings. As long as that reflex lasts, there is a choice available that the pigeoners never took: to pay attention while the thing is still here — not after, when attention curdles into commemoration, and the best we can offer the vanished is a stone, a name, and a sentence that lives forever by not living at all.
